claim: The giant muscle protein titin is a major contributor to passive force.
source: The giant muscle protein titin is a major contributor to passive force; however, its role in active force generation is unresolved.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge about titin's role in passive force.

claim: Titin's role in active force generation is unresolved.
source: The giant muscle protein titin is a major contributor to passive force; however, its role in active force generation is unresolved.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the abstract as a gap in current knowledge.

claim: Under mechanical strain, as titin cleavage doubles from heterozygous to homozygous TC muscles, Z-disks become increasingly out of register.
source: We show that under mechanical strain, as TC doubles from heterozygous to homozygous TC muscles, Z-disks become increasingly out of register while passive and active forces are reduced.
evidence: This finding is reported in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: As titin cleavage doubles from heterozygous to homozygous TC muscles, passive forces are reduced.
source: We show that under mechanical strain, as TC doubles from heterozygous to homozygous TC muscles, Z-disks become increasingly out of register while passive and active forces are reduced.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: As titin cleavage doubles from heterozygous to homozygous TC muscles, active forces are reduced.
source: We show that under mechanical strain, as TC doubles from heterozygous to homozygous TC muscles, Z-disks become increasingly out of register while passive and active forces are reduced.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 6.

claim: Interactions of elastic titin with sarcomeric actin filaments are revealed.
source: Interactions of elastic titin with sarcomeric actin filaments are revealed.
evidence: This finding is stated in the abstract and supported by experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: When titin-cleaved muscles contract, myosin-containing A-bands become split.
source: Strikingly, when titin-cleaved muscles contract, myosin-containing A-bands become split and adjacent myosin filaments move in opposite directions while also shedding myosins.
evidence: This observation is reported in the abstract and supported by electron microscopy images in Figures 6 and 8.

claim: When titin-cleaved muscles contract, adjacent myosin filaments move in opposite directions.
source: Strikingly, when titin-cleaved muscles contract, myosin-containing A-bands become split and adjacent myosin filaments move in opposite directions while also shedding myosins.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by EM images in Figures 6, 7, and 8.

claim: When titin-cleaved muscles contract, myosin filaments shed myosins.
source: Strikingly, when titin-cleaved muscles contract, myosin-containing A-bands become split and adjacent myosin filaments move in opposite directions while also shedding myosins.
evidence: This finding is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Intact titin filaments are critical force-transmission networks that buffer the forces observed by myosin filaments during contraction.
source: This establishes intact titin filaments as critical force-transmission networks, buffering the forces observed by myosin filaments during contraction.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the abstract and inferred from the A-band disruption observed in titin-cleaved contracting muscles.

claim: To perform its force-buffering function, elastic titin must change stiffness or extensible length.
source: To perform this function, elastic titin must change stiffness or extensible length, unveiling its fundamental role as an activation-dependent spring in contracting muscle.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a conclusion based on the observed protective role of titin and mechanical calculations.

claim: Elastic titin has a fundamental role as an activation-dependent spring in contracting muscle.
source: To perform this function, elastic titin must change stiffness or extensible length, unveiling its fundamental role as an activation-dependent spring in contracting muscle.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the abstract based on the findings about titin's mechanical properties during contraction.

claim: Active force of a sarcomere was originally assumed to be entirely generated by the interactions of thick and thin filaments.
source: The theories of muscle contraction were originally developed under the assumption that active force of a muscle cell's contractile unit, the sarcomere, was entirely generated by the interactions of thick and thin filaments (Gordon et al., 1966; Huxley, 1957).
evidence: This is stated as historical context with citations to classic muscle contraction theories.

claim: Titin (also known as connectin) was discovered many years after the original muscle contraction theories were developed.
source: Many years later, a third sarcomeric filament called titin (also known as connectin) was discovered (Maruyama, 1976), and research since then has demonstrated that titin is a critical component of sarcomeric function (Linke, 2018; Nishikawa, 2020).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to the discovery of titin.

claim: Titin is a critical component of sarcomeric function.
source: Many years later, a third sarcomeric filament called titin (also known as connectin) was discovered (Maruyama, 1976), and research since then has demonstrated that titin is a critical component of sarcomeric function (Linke, 2018; Nishikawa, 2020).
evidence: This is stated with citations to recent reviews on titin function.

claim: Titin is the largest known protein.
source: Titin is the largest known protein (Bang et al., 2001) and spans half of the sarcomere from the Z-disk to the M-band.
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Titin spans half of the sarcomere from the Z-disk to the M-band.
source: Titin is the largest known protein (Bang et al., 2001) and spans half of the sarcomere from the Z-disk to the M-band.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about titin structure.

claim: The titin gene is truncated in a substantial proportion of the general population.
source: The titin gene is truncated in a substantial proportion of the general population, and these truncations are frequently associated with cardiomyopathy and occasionally with skeletal myopathies (Linke, 2018).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the clinical relevance.

claim: Titin truncations are frequently associated with cardiomyopathy.
source: The titin gene is truncated in a substantial proportion of the general population, and these truncations are frequently associated with cardiomyopathy and occasionally with skeletal myopathies (Linke, 2018).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the clinical association.

claim: Titin truncations are occasionally associated with skeletal myopathies.
source: The titin gene is truncated in a substantial proportion of the general population, and these truncations are frequently associated with cardiomyopathy and occasionally with skeletal myopathies (Linke, 2018).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the clinical association.

claim: The I-band portion of titin links the thick and thin filaments as an extensible and viscoelastic spring.
source: The I-band portion of titin links the thick and thin filaments as an extensible and viscoelastic spring.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about titin's mechanical properties.

claim: The I-band titin spring produces most, if not all, of the passive force in sarcomeres.
source: While the I-band titin spring produces most, if not all, of the passive force in sarcomeres, the role of titin during active contraction remains undefined, but yet seems critical because the (unspecific) destruction of titin coincides with passive and active tension loss (Higuchi, 1992; Horowits et al., 1986).
evidence: This is stated as current understanding with citations to support the claim.

claim: The role of titin during active contraction remains undefined.
source: While the I-band titin spring produces most, if not all, of the passive force in sarcomeres, the role of titin during active contraction remains undefined, but yet seems critical because the (unspecific) destruction of titin coincides with passive and active tension loss (Higuchi, 1992; Horowits et al., 1986).
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge that the study aims to address.

claim: The destruction of titin coincides with passive and active tension loss.
source: While the I-band titin spring produces most, if not all, of the passive force in sarcomeres, the role of titin during active contraction remains undefined, but yet seems critical because the (unspecific) destruction of titin coincides with passive and active tension loss (Higuchi, 1992; Horowits et al., 1986).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous studies.

claim: Skeletal muscles with genetically modified I-band titin show altered mechanical properties, including muscle stiffness and force.
source: For example, skeletal muscles with genetically modified I-band titin show altered mechanical properties, including muscle stiffness and force, length-dependent activation, and mechanosignaling (Brynnel et al., 2018; Buck et al., 2014; Mateja et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: Skeletal muscles with genetically modified I-band titin show altered length-dependent activation.
source: For example, skeletal muscles with genetically modified I-band titin show altered mechanical properties, including muscle stiffness and force, length-dependent activation, and mechanosignaling (Brynnel et al., 2018; Buck et al., 2014; Mateja et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: Skeletal muscles with genetically modified I-band titin show altered mechanosignaling.
source: For example, skeletal muscles with genetically modified I-band titin show altered mechanical properties, including muscle stiffness and force, length-dependent activation, and mechanosignaling (Brynnel et al., 2018; Buck et al., 2014; Mateja et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: A relationship between titin-based and actomyosin-based forces has been suggested to optimize the work generated by muscle contraction.
source: A relationship between titin-based and actomyosin-based forces has been suggested to optimize the work generated by muscle contraction (Rivas-Pardo et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the hypothesis.

claim: Direct empirical evidence into titin-based regulation of active contraction is limited.
source: However, direct empirical evidence into titin-based regulation of active contraction is limited.
evidence: This is stated as justification for the current study.

claim: Almost all animal models with a mutational change in titin present a phenotype of muscle dystrophy and wasting.
source: However, almost all animal models with a mutational change in titin present a phenotype of muscle dystrophy and wasting (e.g. Radke et al., 2019; Swist et al., 2020), and all previous methods to degrade titin also degrade other proteins (Horowits, 1999).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the limitation of previous approaches.

claim: All previous methods to degrade titin also degrade other proteins.
source: However, almost all animal models with a mutational change in titin present a phenotype of muscle dystrophy and wasting (e.g. Radke et al., 2019; Swist et al., 2020), and all previous methods to degrade titin also degrade other proteins (Horowits, 1999).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the limitation of previous methods.

claim: A new mouse model was generated with a cloned-in HaloTag-TEV cassette inserted into I-band titin close to the A-band.
source: To mitigate the problems outlined above, a new mouse model was generated with a cloned-in HaloTag-TEV cassette inserted into I-band titin close to the A-band (Rivas-Pardo et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to the original description of the mouse model.

claim: The tobacco etch virus (TEV) protease-recognition site is specifically cleaved by the TEV protease.
source: The tobacco etch virus (TEV) protease-recognition site is specifically cleaved by the TEV protease, while the HaloTag domain allows for easy protein labeling, useful, for example, for the assessment of titin cleaving.
evidence: This is stated as a property of the TEV protease system.

claim: The HaloTag domain allows for easy protein labeling.
source: The tobacco etch virus (TEV) protease-recognition site is specifically cleaved by the TEV protease, while the HaloTag domain allows for easy protein labeling, useful, for example, for the assessment of titin cleaving.
evidence: This is stated as a property of the HaloTag system.

claim: The HaloTag-TEV insertion does not affect mouse development, muscle structure, or performance.
source: The insertion itself does not affect mouse development, muscle structure, or performance (Rivas-Pardo et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to the original characterization of the mouse model.

claim: Heterozygous TC fibers contain approximately 50% of HaloTag-TEV titins compared to homozygous TC fibers.
source: These data show that on average, approximately 50% of HaloTag-TEV titins are present in Het fibers and that these molecules are effectively cleaved by TEV protease.
evidence: This conclusion is stated based on multiple quantification methods shown in Figure 1.

claim: HaloTag-TEV titins in heterozygous fibers are effectively cleaved by TEV protease.
source: These data show that on average, approximately 50% of HaloTag-TEV titins are present in Het fibers and that these molecules are effectively cleaved by TEV protease.
evidence: This is stated based on gel electrophoresis data in Figure 1E.

claim: Het TC fibers produced 57.3% of normalized HaloTag IF staining intensity compared to Hom TC fibers.
source: Het produced 57.3% of normalized HaloTag IF staining intensity compared to Hom TC fibers (Het: 32.08 ± 0.90) arbitrary units (a.u.; mean ± SEM, Hom: 55.95 ± 0.64 a.u.; Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by quantification shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Het TC fibers contained 36.8% of Hom HaloTag antibody-conjugated nanogold particles on IEM images.
source: When comparing the label abundance of HaloTag antibody-conjugated nanogold particles on IEM images between genotypes, Het contained 36.8% of Hom (Het: 34.42 ± 2.42 a.u., Hom: 93.60 ± 1.98 a.u., Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by quantification shown in Figure 1D.

claim: After TEV protease treatment, two smaller titin bands were visible in Het and Hom TC muscles at approximately 2.3 MDa for A-M-band titin and approximately 1.4 MDa for Z-I-band titin.
source: Compared to a single N2A titin band (~3.7 MDa) in control samples (including treated and untreated Wt), after TEV protease treatment, two smaller bands were clearly visible in Het and Hom TC muscles at the expected sizes of ~2.3 MDa for A-M-band titin and ~1.4 MDa for Z-I-band titin, indicating specific titin cleavage.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Densitometric analysis confirmed full cleavage in Hom fibers and revealed 43.12 ± 0.85% cleaved titins in Het.
source: Densitometric analysis of intact and A-M-band titin intensities confirmed full cleavage in Hom fibers and revealed 43.12 ± 0.85% cleaved titins in Het (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by quantification shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Western blotting showed that the proportion of mutant titins in Het was 49.86 ± 1.24% of Hom (100.00 ± 5.51%).
source: We found that the proportion of mutant titins in Het was 49.86 ± 1.24% (n = 29) of Hom (100.00 ± 5.51%; n = 13) (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Titin cleavage readily resulted in a length-dependent decrease of passive tension in Het and Hom TC fibers, but not Wt fibers.
source: Titin cleavage readily resulted in a length-dependent decrease of passive tension in Het and Hom TC fibers, but not Wt fibers (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Both elastic and viscous force components were reduced in the mutant genotypes after titin cleavage, more so in Hom than in Het.
source: Both components were reduced in the mutant genotypes after titin cleavage, more so in Hom than in Het (Figure 2B,D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 2B and 2D.

claim: The relative force decreases in Hom vs. Wt typically reached approximately 50-55% at SLs between 2.6 and 3.2 µm.
source: The relative force decreases in Hom vs. Wt typically reached ~50–55% at SLs between 2.6 and 3.2 µm.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on the data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Negative correlations between passive force and intact titin were strongest (R2 > 0.5) at moderate or long SLs.
source: We found that negative correlations were strongest (R2 > 0.5) at moderate or long SLs, with the slope of the regression becoming steeper at the longer SLs.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 2C and 2E.

claim: At the shortest SLs, weak correlations (R2 < 0.5) were found between passive force and intact titin.
source: At the shortest SLs, we found weak correlations (R2 < 0.5) as forces were always close to 0, which is in line with the relatively small titin- or fiber-based passive forces at these lengths, as well as the non-linear nature of the titin force–SL relationship (Prado et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the text with a citation and shown in Figures 2C and 2E.

claim: In glycerol-skinned fiber preparations, some but not all extra-myofibril components to passive force are removed.
source: Note that in glycerol-skinned fiber preparations, some but not all extra-myofibril components to passive force are removed; thus, non-titin contributions to passive force will be realized in passive force traces.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological consideration.

claim: Nearly 50% of passive elastic forces remained in treated Hom fibers between 2.4 and 3.2 μm SL.
source: Indeed, non-titin force components clearly appeared in treated Hom fibers, where nearly 50% of passive elastic forces remained between 2.4 and 3.2 μm SL and >50% remained at 3.4 μm SL.
evidence: This is stated based on the data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Residual forces after titin cleavage in Hom skinned fibers are presumably due to strained intracellular and/or extramyofibrillar structures.
source: These residual forces after titin cleavage in Hom skinned fibers are presumably due to strained intracellular (e.g. microtubules; Kerr et al., 2015) and/or extramyofibrillar structures (Prado et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation with citations to support the claim.

claim: Titin loss in Hom fibers increased the indentation depth at 3 nN indentation force approximately 33% from 295.90 ± 5.97 nm to 392.70 ± 11.60 nm.
source: We found that titin loss in Hom fibers increased the indentation depth at 3 nN indentation force ~33% from 295.90 ± 5.97 nm to 392.70 ± 11.60 nm, and the Young's modulus decreased ~33% from 4.81 ± 0.15 kPa to 3.24 ± 0.15 kPa (mean ± SEM; n = 34/38 recordings for Hom/Wt) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Titin loss in Hom fibers decreased the Young's modulus approximately 33% from 4.81 ± 0.15 kPa to 3.24 ± 0.15 kPa.
source: We found that titin loss in Hom fibers increased the indentation depth at 3 nN indentation force ~33% from 295.90 ± 5.97 nm to 392.70 ± 11.60 nm, and the Young's modulus decreased ~33% from 4.81 ± 0.15 kPa to 3.24 ± 0.15 kPa (mean ± SEM; n = 34/38 recordings for Hom/Wt) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Titin-based transverse stiffness is an important component of cellular transverse stiffness in skinned skeletal fibers.
source: Thus, titin-based transverse stiffness is an important component of cellular transverse stiffness in skinned skeletal fibers.
evidence: This conclusion is stated based on the AFM data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Radial compressive forces are relatively less dependent on intact titin stiffness than longitudinal stretch forces.
source: However, radial compressive forces are relatively less dependent on intact titin stiffness than longitudinal stretch forces.
evidence: This conclusion is stated based on comparison of AFM data (Figure 3) and passive stretch data (Figure 2).

claim: TEV-protease rapidly decreased passive force for the first 10 min after its addition to Het or Hom TC fibers.
source: We found that, compared to control trials, TEV-protease rapidly decreased passive force for the first 10 min after its addition to Het or Hom TC fibers (Figure 4A, middle).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Most cleavable titins were severed after approximately 10 min of TEV protease treatment.
source: Thereafter, the kinetics were similar to Wt fibers, indicating that most cleavable titins were severed after ~10 min of treatment, slightly faster than previously reported by us (Rivas-Pardo et al., 2020), due probably to different activities of the TEV-protease batches used.
evidence: This is stated based on the kinetics data shown in Figure 4A, with a citation to previous work.

claim: In Het TC samples, TEV-protease treatment removed titin-based forces accounting for 21.42 ± 4.26% of total passive force.
source: In Het and Hom (but not Wt) TC samples, TEV-protease treatment removed titin-based forces accounting for 21.42 ± 4.26% and 67.44 ± 1.46%, respectively, of total passive force (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: In Hom TC samples, TEV-protease treatment removed titin-based forces accounting for 67.44 ± 1.46% of total passive force.
source: In Het and Hom (but not Wt) TC samples, TEV-protease treatment removed titin-based forces accounting for 21.42 ± 4.26% and 67.44 ± 1.46%, respectively, of total passive force (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: TEV protease-treated Het and Hom TC fibers revealed A-band disorder (streaming) and Z-disks that lost their typical linear appearance.
source: Wt fibers treated with TEV protease appeared structurally normal, whereas TEV protease-treated Het and Hom TC fibers revealed A-band disorder (streaming) and Z-disks that lost their typical linear appearance.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: TEV protease-treated Het fibers had a modest increase in fracture area compared to WT fibers.
source: According to this analysis, when compared to the WT fibers, TEV protease-treated Het fibers had a modest increase in fracture area, whereas Hom fibers showed substantial Z-disk disorder, with large variability (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4D.

claim: TEV protease-treated Hom fibers showed substantial Z-disk disorder, with large variability.
source: According to this analysis, when compared to the WT fibers, TEV protease-treated Het fibers had a modest increase in fracture area, whereas Hom fibers showed substantial Z-disk disorder, with large variability (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The decrease in Z-disk linearity with progressive titin cleavage demonstrates the importance of titin-based forces in balancing out the I-bands on opposite sides of a Z-disk.
source: Taken together, the observed decrease in Z-disk linearity with progressive titin cleavage demonstrates the importance of titin-based forces in balancing out the I-bands on opposite sides of a Z-disk, which is an interesting, previously unrecognized, property of titin.
evidence: This conclusion is stated based on the Z-disk disorder data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The proximal T12 labels remained stationary upon titin cleavage, relative to the Z-disk.
source: On immunoelectron micrographs, the proximal T12 labels (nanogold particles) remained stationary upon titin cleavage, relative to the Z-disk, whereas the two other more distal antibody labels were partially translocated toward the Z-disk, indicating titin recoil (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The N2A and PEVK antibody labels were partially translocated toward the Z-disk upon titin cleavage, indicating titin recoil.
source: On immunoelectron micrographs, the proximal T12 labels (nanogold particles) remained stationary upon titin cleavage, relative to the Z-disk, whereas the two other more distal antibody labels were partially translocated toward the Z-disk, indicating titin recoil (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5B.

claim: In Het fibers, a bimodal distribution appeared for N2A and PEVK epitopes, with some epitopes remaining at the normal position and others recoiling partially or fully back to the Z-disk.
source: In Het fibers, a bimodal distribution appeared, with some epitopes remaining at the normal position and others recoiling partially or fully back to the Z-disk.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Even in Hom fibers, full titin recoil was not achieved by many titin molecules.
source: Interestingly, even in Hom fibers, full titin recoil was not achieved by many titin molecules, as reflected by a high variability in recoil distance for N2A and PEVK epitopes (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Full titin recoil was not achieved likely because titin stuck to the surrounding proteins of the thin filament.
source: Full titin recoil was not achieved, likely because titin stuck to the surrounding proteins of the thin filament, a known interaction point in in vitro preparations (Kulke et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation with a citation to support the titin-actin interaction.

claim: TEV-only treated cardiomyocytes demonstrated partial titin recoil, as in skeletal fibers.
source: Strikingly, while TEV-only treated cardiomyocytes demonstrated partial titin recoil, as in skeletal fibers, the removal of actin filaments allowed cleaved titins to recoil all the way to the Z-disk (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The removal of actin filaments allowed cleaved titins to recoil all the way to the Z-disk.
source: Strikingly, while TEV-only treated cardiomyocytes demonstrated partial titin recoil, as in skeletal fibers, the removal of actin filaments allowed cleaved titins to recoil all the way to the Z-disk (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Titin can inherently recoil to the Z-disk, but in many molecules, titin–thin filament interactions inhibit this action.
source: We conclude that titin can inherently recoil to the Z-disk, but that in many molecules, titin–thin filament interactions inhibit this action.
evidence: This conclusion is stated based on the gelsolin treatment experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: TEV treatment after the first contraction significantly reduced active force of the second contraction by 22.83 ± 2.78% in Het fibers.
source: However, TEV treatment after the first contraction significantly reduced active force of the second contraction by 22.83 ± 2.78% and 46.31 ± 2.68% in Het and Hom fibers, respectively (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6B.

claim: TEV treatment after the first contraction significantly reduced active force of the second contraction by 46.31 ± 2.68% in Hom fibers.
source: However, TEV treatment after the first contraction significantly reduced active force of the second contraction by 22.83 ± 2.78% and 46.31 ± 2.68% in Het and Hom fibers, respectively (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Titin-based stiffness is crucial to maintaining high active force levels during muscle contraction.
source: Thus, titin-based stiffness is crucial to maintaining high active force levels during muscle contraction.
evidence: This conclusion is stated based on the active force reduction data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Het and Hom fibers showed progressive disorganization of Z-disks and A-bands after contraction with 50% and 100% cleaved titins, respectively.
source: Het and Hom fibers showed progressive disorganization of Z-disks and A-bands after contraction with 50% and 100% cleaved titins, respectively (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6C.

claim: After titin cleavage, individual A-bands showed a streaming effect of the electron-dense material and a loss of the typical M-band structures.
source: However, after titin cleavage, individual A-bands showed a streaming effect of the electron-dense material and a loss of the typical M-band structures (Figure 6C), all indicative of a loss of A-band protein order.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Single or groups of adjacent thick filaments detached from the M-band complex and from one another and traveled in opposite directions until driven against the Z-disks.
source: Remarkably, these images suggested that single or groups of adjacent thick filaments detached from the M-band complex and from one another and traveled in opposite directions until driven against the Z-disks.
evidence: This is stated based on interpretation of EM images in Figure 6C.

claim: Hom, and to a lesser extent Het fibers, presented thick filaments that appeared shorter than normal (<1.6 μm).
source: Furthermore, Hom, and to a lesser extent Het fibers, presented thick filaments that appeared shorter than normal (<1.6 μm), as if the myosin molecules were being shed from the tips of the thick filaments.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on EM observations in Figure 6C.

claim: The titin/NEB ratio of contracting fibers was largely unaffected by titin cleavage.
source: In spite of substantial data scatter, general trends were apparent: the titin/NEB ratio of contracting fibers was largely unaffected by titin cleavage (Wt+TEV: 1.90 ± 1.15; Het+TEV: 2.19 ± 1.13; Hom+TEV: 1.19 ± 0.93), whereas the MyHC/titin ratio tended to be reduced (Wt+TEV: 13.72 ± 4.91; Het+TEV: 5.67 ± 2.05; Hom+TEV: 8.82 ± 4.71), and this trend was even stronger for the MyHC/NEB ratio (Wt+TEV: 11.03 ± 3.36; Het+TEV: 5.37 ± 1.38; Hom+TEV: 3.475 ± 1.73; p=0.081, Wt vs. Hom).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The MyHC/titin ratio tended to be reduced after titin cleavage and contraction.
source: In spite of substantial data scatter, general trends were apparent: the titin/NEB ratio of contracting fibers was largely unaffected by titin cleavage (Wt+TEV: 1.90 ± 1.15; Het+TEV: 2.19 ± 1.13; Hom+TEV: 1.19 ± 0.93), whereas the MyHC/titin ratio tended to be reduced (Wt+TEV: 13.72 ± 4.91; Het+TEV: 5.67 ± 2.05; Hom+TEV: 8.82 ± 4.71), and this trend was even stronger for the MyHC/NEB ratio (Wt+TEV: 11.03 ± 3.36; Het+TEV: 5.37 ± 1.38; Hom+TEV: 3.475 ± 1.73; p=0.081, Wt vs. Hom).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The MyHC/NEB ratio showed a stronger reduction trend after titin cleavage and contraction (p=0.081, Wt vs. Hom).
source: In spite of substantial data scatter, general trends were apparent: the titin/NEB ratio of contracting fibers was largely unaffected by titin cleavage (Wt+TEV: 1.90 ± 1.15; Het+TEV: 2.19 ± 1.13; Hom+TEV: 1.19 ± 0.93), whereas the MyHC/titin ratio tended to be reduced (Wt+TEV: 13.72 ± 4.91; Het+TEV: 5.67 ± 2.05; Hom+TEV: 8.82 ± 4.71), and this trend was even stronger for the MyHC/NEB ratio (Wt+TEV: 11.03 ± 3.36; Het+TEV: 5.37 ± 1.38; Hom+TEV: 3.475 ± 1.73; p=0.081, Wt vs. Hom).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Myosin molecules are free to float out into solution following titin cleavage and active contraction.
source: These findings suggest that myosin molecules are free to float out into solution following titin cleavage and active contraction, emphasizing that contraction with cleaved I-band titin leads to rapid A-band destruction.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the protein ratio data in Figure 6D.

claim: A-band length is smaller after contraction of TEV-treated Het fibers and even shorter for Hom fibers.
source: We found that A-band length is smaller after contraction of TEV-treated Het fibers and even shorter for Hom fibers.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 7D.

claim: With titin cleavage, MYOM and HaloTag sites began to overlap in Het fibers.
source: In non-treated (Het) fibers, the MYOM band was cleanly centered between the two HaloTag bands (Figure 7A). However, with titin cleavage, MYOM and HaloTag sites began to overlap in Het fibers (Figure 7B), and were completely intermingled in Hom fibers, seemingly covering the entire A-band region (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 7B.

claim: In Hom fibers with titin cleavage, MYOM and HaloTag sites were completely intermingled, seemingly covering the entire A-band region.
source: In non-treated (Het) fibers, the MYOM band was cleanly centered between the two HaloTag bands (Figure 7A). However, with titin cleavage, MYOM and HaloTag sites began to overlap in Het fibers (Figure 7B), and were completely intermingled in Hom fibers, seemingly covering the entire A-band region (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The MYOM-containing M-band appeared to lose its structure and broaden after titin cleavage.
source: Thus, the MYOM-containing M-band appeared to lose its structure and broaden.
evidence: This conclusion is stated based on the IF data shown in Figure 7.

claim: A lack of titin-based forces leads to individual thick filaments being pulled out of their regularly aligned arrangement in the A-band and moving toward the Z-disks.
source: These observations present evidence that a lack of titin-based forces leads to (1) the individual thick filaments being pulled out of their regularly aligned arrangement in the A-band and moving toward the Z-disks (an extreme case of A-band 'streaming') and (2) individual myosin molecules becoming detached from the tips of the thick filament (including the D-zone), most likely as a by-product of the force generated by crossbridge binding to actin.
evidence: This conclusion is stated based on the EM observations in Figures 6-8.

claim: A lack of titin-based forces leads to individual myosin molecules becoming detached from the tips of the thick filament.
source: These observations present evidence that a lack of titin-based forces leads to (1) the individual thick filaments being pulled out of their regularly aligned arrangement in the A-band and moving toward the Z-disks (an extreme case of A-band 'streaming') and (2) individual myosin molecules becoming detached from the tips of the thick filament (including the D-zone), most likely as a by-product of the force generated by crossbridge binding to actin.
evidence: This conclusion is stated based on the EM observations in Figures 6-8.

claim: Titin is a critical component to A-band stability during contraction.
source: Collectively, our data demonstrate that titin is a critical component to A-band stability during contraction.
evidence: This conclusion is stated based on the A-band disruption observed in contracting titin-cleaved fibers.

claim: Titin-based passive stretch forces in permeabilized fibers scale linearly with the proportion of intact titin springs.
source: From our data, we draw the following main conclusions: (1) Titin-based passive stretch forces in permeabilized fibers scale linearly with the proportion of intact titin springs.
evidence: This is stated as a main conclusion in the Discussion based on data in Figure 2.

claim: Titin contributes at least one-half of the passive viscous and elastic forces of permeabilized fibers in the longitudinal direction.
source: (2) Titin contributes at least one-half of the passive viscous and elastic forces of permeabilized fibers in the longitudinal direction.
evidence: This is stated as a main conclusion in the Discussion based on data in Figure 2.

claim: Titin stiffness is critical for maintaining Z-disk organization and structure under mechanical stress.
source: (3) Titin stiffness is critical for maintaining Z-disk organization and structure under mechanical stress.
evidence: This is stated as a main conclusion in the Discussion based on data in Figure 4.

claim: Cleaved titins not only recoil toward the Z-disk elastically but also bind to thin filaments.
source: (4) Cleaved titins not only recoil toward the Z-disk elastically but also bind to thin filaments.
evidence: This is stated as a main conclusion in the Discussion based on data in Figure 5.

claim: Titin-based forces are crucial to maintaining high active contractile forces.
source: (5) Titin-based forces are crucial to maintaining high active contractile forces.
evidence: This is stated as a main conclusion in the Discussion based on data in Figure 6.

claim: When titin-cleaved Het and Hom TC fibers contract, individual thick filaments quickly begin to separate from each other and travel toward the Z-disks.
source: (6) When titin-cleaved Het and Hom TC fibers contract, individual thick filaments quickly begin to separate from each other and travel toward the Z-disks.
evidence: This is stated as a main conclusion in the Discussion based on data in Figures 6-8.

claim: Myosin shedding from the thick-filament tips functionally shortens the thick filaments, sometimes up to almost their entire length.
source: In parallel, myosin shedding from the thick-filament tips functionally shortens the thick filaments, sometimes up to almost their entire length.
evidence: This is stated as a main conclusion in the Discussion based on data in Figures 6-8.

claim: Titin serves a protective role by preventing active forces from disrupting the A-band organization.
source: Taken together, these findings indicate that titin serves a protective role by preventing active forces from disrupting the A-band organization.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the Discussion based on the overall findings.

claim: The passive force magnitude and the SL at which passive force is measurable are correlated with titin size and stiffness.
source: It is well established that the passive force magnitude and the SL at which passive force is measurable are correlated with titin size and stiffness (Brynnel et al., 2018; Mateja et al., 2013; Prado et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Unspecific titin degradation by trypsin or ionizing radiation in skinned fibers leads to passive force reductions proportional to the amount of titin destroyed.
source: Furthermore, unspecific titin degradation by trypsin or ionizing radiation in skinned fibers leads to passive force reductions proportional to the amount of titin destroyed (Higuchi, 1992; Horowits et al., 1986).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous studies.

claim: A linear relationship between the number of intact titin springs and titin-based passive force is clearly supported by the results.
source: A linear relationship between the number of intact titin springs and titin-based passive force is clearly supported by our results.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the data in Figure 2.

claim: If all titins are cleaved in permeabilized Hom fibers, passive forces drop by a little over 50%, except at the extreme extensions.
source: If all titins are cleaved in permeabilized Hom fibers, passive forces drop by a little over 50%, except at the extreme extensions, when other load-bearing elements (e.g. remnant extracellular matrix proteins; Prado et al., 2005) become relatively more important.
evidence: This is stated based on the data in Figure 2, with a citation for other load-bearing elements.

claim: In Hom fibers held in a high-stretch state, titin cleavage caused an over-proportionate decrease (~67%) in passive force.
source: Surprisingly, in Hom fibers held in a high-stretch state, titin cleavage caused an over-proportionate decrease (~67%) in passive force.
evidence: This is stated based on the data in Figure 4.

claim: The TEV-cleavage site is located in the distal Ig region, where six titin molecules engage in inter-titin interactions for approximately 100 nm, making up the 'end-filament'.
source: The TEV-cleavage site is located in the distal Ig region, where six titin molecules engage in inter-titin interactions for ~100 nm, making up the 'end-filament' (Liversage et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the structural description.

claim: Beyond the end-filament, in the direction of the Z-disk, titin molecules divide into dimers or monomers.
source: Beyond the end-filament, in the direction of the Z-disk, titin molecules divide into dimers or monomers (Kötter et al., 2014); in the opposite direction, they probably run as dimers along the thick filament (Zoghbi et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the structural description.

claim: Titin molecules probably run as dimers along the thick filament.
source: Beyond the end-filament, in the direction of the Z-disk, titin molecules divide into dimers or monomers (Kötter et al., 2014); in the opposite direction, they probably run as dimers along the thick filament (Zoghbi et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the structural description.

claim: In Hom fibers that are held at the long length for an extended time and then TEV treated, all six end-filament titins (per half-thick filament) may retract as a unit.
source: However, in Hom fibers that are held at the long length for an extended time and then TEV treated, all six end-filament titins (per half-thick filament) may retract as a unit, presumably explaining the relatively large drop in passive force.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation to explain the over-proportionate force decrease.

claim: Others have estimated that titin generates >90% of total passive longitudinal force in skinned psoas fibers, when assessed using high-salt extraction baths.
source: Others have estimated that titin generates >90% of total passive longitudinal force in skinned psoas fibers, when assessed using high-salt extraction baths (Brynnel et al., 2018; Irving et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous studies.

claim: High-salt solutions have the disadvantage of also removing other proteins that are potentially load bearing (i.e. intermediate filaments).
source: These high-salt solutions have the disadvantage of also removing other proteins that are potentially load bearing (i.e. intermediate filaments).
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of previous methods.

claim: In the physiological operating range (<3.4 µm SL), titin contributes less than 70%, but over 50%, of total longitudinal force in permeabilized fibers.
source: Therefore, we provide an update to the current knowledge that in the physiological operating range (<3.4 µm SL), titin contributes less than 70%, but over 50%, of total longitudinal force in permeabilized fibers.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the data in Figure 2.

claim: Longitudinal, permeabilized fiber transverse stiffness depends to a lesser degree on intact titin, which is responsible for approximately one-third of this stiffness.
source: In contrast to longitudinal, permeabilized fiber transverse stiffness depends to a lesser degree on intact titin, which is responsible for approximately one-third of this stiffness.
evidence: This is stated based on the AFM data in Figure 3.

claim: Other contributors to myocyte stiffness, especially transverse compressive stiffness, may include the microtubules, the desmin intermediate filaments, and the non-sarcomeric actin filament (microfilament) network.
source: Other contributors to myocyte stiffness, especially transverse compressive stiffness, may include the microtubules (Kerr et al., 2015), the desmin intermediate filaments (Charrier et al., 2018), and the non-sarcomeric actin filament (microfilament) network (Wang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim about other contributors.

claim: Glycerol permeabilization procedures on fibers degrade some, but not all, of these extramyofibrillar structures.
source: Glycerol permeabilization procedures on fibers (performed in the current work) degrade some, but not all, of these extramyofibrillar structures, and so their contributions to fiber stiffness will probably be greater for intact fibers or whole muscles (Brynnel et al., 2018; Irving et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the methodological consideration.

claim: In TEV-treated passive muscle fibers, cleaved titin recoiled toward the Z-disk but also got stuck to thin filaments along the way.
source: In TEV-treated passive muscle fibers, cleaved titin recoiled toward the Z-disk but also got stuck to thin filaments along the way.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of findings from Figure 5.

claim: The data are in agreement with the hypotheses that titin functionalities in muscle contraction include titin-actin interactions.
source: Our data are in agreement with the hypotheses that titin functionalities in muscle contraction include titin-actin interactions (Linke, 2018; Nishikawa, 2020), which have previously been observed in molecular and myofibril preparations (Dutta et al., 2018; Kulke et al., 2001; Nagy et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the interpretation.

claim: Although titin-based passive forces are frequently not detectable <2.5 μm SL in skeletal muscle, they must be present even at shorter SLs, as titin was able to recoil all the way to the Z-disk.
source: Another interesting implication of our finding is that although titin-based passive forces are frequently not detectable <2.5 μm SL in skeletal muscle (Linke et al., 1998a; Prado et al., 2005), they must be present even at shorter SLs, as titin was able to recoil all the way to the Z-disk.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the recoil data, with citations to previous studies.

claim: Titin always has some level of force that can contribute to Z-disk alignment and A-band centering at any SL, at least down to approximately 1.8 μm SL, where the I-band disappears as thick filaments drive into the Z-disk.
source: This makes it clear that titin always has some level of force that can contribute to Z-disk alignment and A-band centering at any SL, at least down to ~1.8 μm SL, where the I-band disappears as thick filaments drive into the Z-disk.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the recoil findings.

claim: Titin has long been thought to maintain A-band stability during and after active muscle contraction.
source: Titin has long been thought to maintain A-band stability during and after active muscle contraction (Higuchi, 1992; Horowits et al., 1986).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous studies.

claim: Horowits et al., 1986 used EM and graded radiation-induced titin destruction to demonstrate that titin plays a critical role in centering the A-band complex.
source: Horowits et al., 1986 used EM and graded radiation-induced titin destruction to demonstrate that titin plays a critical role in centering the A-band complex.
evidence: This is stated with a citation to the classic study.

claim: Specific cleavage of the titin springs reduces active forces dramatically and the tension loss correlates to the amount of titin being cleaved.
source: We show, for the first time, that specific cleavage of the titin springs reduces active forces dramatically and that the tension loss correlates to the amount of titin being cleaved.
evidence: This is stated as a novel finding based on data in Figure 6.

claim: The 12 titin molecules (six titins per half-thick filament) have long been thought to produce a centering force against thick-filament movement.
source: Because of their location around a thick filament, the 12 titin molecules (six titins per half-thick filament; Liversage et al., 2001) have long been thought to produce a centering force against thick-filament movement (Horowits, 1999).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the hypothesis.

claim: The A-band is made up of approximately 500 parallel thick filaments per μm2 cross-sectional area that sit in register and are connected at the M-band through force-bearing M-bridges, predominately made up of myomesin.
source: The A-band is made up of ~500 parallel thick filaments per μm2 cross-sectional area that sit in register and are connected at the M-band through force-bearing M-bridges, predominately made up of myomesin (Lange et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the structural description.

claim: At rest, all thick filaments are radially and longitudinally centered in a sarcomere by titin-based forces.
source: At rest, all thick filaments are radially and longitudinally centered in a sarcomere by titin-based forces (Horowits, 1999), and so tension on the M-band structures, caused by adjacent thick filaments, is ~0 pN.
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Thin filament length variability can be as large as 100 nm.
source: Importantly, because of thin filament length variability as large as 100 nm (Littlefield and Fowler, 2002), the force producing region between each half-thick filament and thin filament is variable at the immediate onset of contraction.
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: M-band structures can extend up to 70 nm at low force.
source: Thick-filament movement away from a central position is exacerbated by M-band structures, which can extend up to 70 nm at low force (Berkemeier et al., 2011; Xiao and Gräter, 2014), allowing thick-filament movement toward the stronger side of the sarcomere during active contraction and enhancing force imbalances especially during prolonged contractions.
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: Forces on M-bridges are conservatively estimated to be <50 pN (0–6.25% maximal force at optimal overlap, P0) on average, with pockets that could reach as high as 120 pN (~25% P0) at 2.6–2.7 µm SL.
source: Considering this within the context of sarcomere geometry, filament overlap, and structural mechanics between thick filaments, we conservatively estimate forces on M-bridges are <50 pN (0–6.25% maximal force at optimal overlap, P0) on average, with pockets that could reach as high as 120 pN (~25% P0) at 2.6–2.7 µm SL.
evidence: This is stated as a calculation based on sarcomere mechanics.

claim: There are six titin filaments per half-thick filament.
source: On the other side of the equation, there are the six titin filaments per half-thick filament (Liversage et al., 2001), and their forces have been estimated from passive myofibril mechanics (Linke et al., 1998b).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the structural description.

claim: Thick-filament movement within A-bands will lead to a titin length change of approximately 35 nm and generate a titin-based centering force in psoas of approximately 12 pN/molecule at 2.65 μm SL.
source: Thick-filament movement within A-bands will lead to a titin length change of ~35 nm (six lengthening on one side/six shortening on the other side) and generate a titin-based centering force in psoas of ~12 pN/molecule at 2.65 μm SL (Linke et al., 1998b; Prado et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the calculation.

claim: Titin-based centering forces are up to an order of magnitude smaller than potential thick-filament movement forces.
source: Based on this first approximation, titin-based centering forces are up to an order of magnitude smaller than potential thick-filament movement forces.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the force calculations.

claim: To produce 120 pN of centering force and provide A-band stability, active titin stiffness would need to be approximately 4x larger than measured in passive muscle.
source: To produce 120 pN of centering force against our upper estimate of thick filament force, and provide A-band stability, active titin stiffness would need to be approximately 4x larger than measured in passive muscle.
evidence: This is stated as a calculation based on the force requirements.

claim: Recent hypotheses in muscle contraction purport that titin undergoes a structural rearrangement during contraction that leads to actin binding at or around the N2A/PEVK regions upon activation.
source: Interestingly, recent hypotheses in muscle contraction purport that titin undergoes a structural rearrangement during contraction that leads to actin binding at or around the N2A/PEVK regions upon activation (Dutta et al., 2018; Kulke et al., 2001; Nagy et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the hypothesis.

claim: The functional extensibility of I-band titin is thought to change so that only the stiffer PEVK region, and not the more compliant proximal Ig region, is extensible during contraction.
source: Consequently, the functional extensibility of I-band titin is thought to change so that only the stiffer PEVK region, and not the more compliant proximal Ig region, is extensible (Linke, 2018; Nishikawa, 2020; Powers et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the hypothesis.

claim: The structural change of titin during contraction has the effect of increasing titin stiffness by fourfold to sixfold.
source: This structural change has the effect of increasing titin stiffness by fourfold to sixfold (Nishikawa, 2020), which is in agreement with our estimation that titin must become up to fourfold stiffer in active, compared to passive, permeabilized fibers.
evidence: This is stated with a citation and compared to the calculations in the current study.

claim: The atomic structure of the thick filament remains to be fully resolved in mammalian muscles.
source: The atomic structure of the thick filament remains to be fully resolved in mammalian muscles (Irving, 2017; Zoghbi et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: The central portion of the thick filament contains an even volume of myosin proteins, whereas the last approximately 160 nm of the thick-filament ends (including the D-zone) taper down until only a few myosin proteins are left.
source: However, we do know that the central portion of the thick filament contains an even volume of myosin proteins, whereas the last ~160 nm of the thick-filament ends (including the D-zone; Figure 8) taper down until only a few myosin proteins are left, in a potentially unstabilized manner.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about thick filament structure.

claim: The six titin filaments that run along the half-thick filament all converge at the end of the thick filament into the end-filament.
source: Because the six titin filaments that run along the half-thick filament all converge at the end of the thick filament into the end-filament (Houmeida et al., 2008), it is not difficult to consider that this region of titin can help stabilize the tips of the thick filaments (Tskhovrebova and Trinick, 2017).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the structural description.

claim: The end-filament region of titin can help stabilize the tips of the thick filaments.
source: Because the six titin filaments that run along the half-thick filament all converge at the end of the thick filament into the end-filament (Houmeida et al., 2008), it is not difficult to consider that this region of titin can help stabilize the tips of the thick filaments (Tskhovrebova and Trinick, 2017).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the hypothesis.

claim: In zebrafish containing an A-band titin null mutation, prenatal sarcomeres assemble normally, but quickly degrade at the start of prenatal contractile activity.
source: This view is supported by the findings in zebrafish containing an A-band titin null mutation, where prenatal sarcomeres assemble normally, but quickly degrade at the start of prenatal contractile activity, indicating a lack of structural stability and a need for titin proteins for stabilization (Myhre et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.
